analysis.one_liner: Bars companies from owning a pharmacy and an insurer or pharmacy benefit manager at the same time.
analysis.headline: Introduced 23 days before the end of the 118th Congress, the bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for one company to own a pharmacy and also own a health insurer or a pharmacy benefit manager — the middlemen that negotiate drug prices and decide which pharmacies can serve an insurance plan's customers. A few large companies currently combine all three, steering patients toward their own pharmacies. Companies that did this would have had three years to sell off their pharmacies, and federal and state enforcers could sue violators and claw back pharmacy revenue earned during the violation, with recovered money directed to communities that were overcharged.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who fill prescriptions, especially at independent drugstores. The bill aimed at the practice of insurers and pharmacy benefit managers owning the pharmacies they steer patients to, which can raise what patients pay and squeeze community pharmacies out of the market. Independent and community pharmacies would compete against companies that no longer both write the rules and own the competition.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Prescription drug customers and independent pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any person from owning or operating a pharmacy while also owning an insurance company or a pharmacy benefit manager, and gives violators three years to divest the pharmacy [S2]

Lets the FTC, the Justice Department antitrust division, the HHS Inspector General, or a state attorney general sue violators, force divestment, and disgorge pharmacy revenue earned during the violation [S2]

Directs that disgorged revenue be placed in an FTC-administered fund used to serve the health care needs of the harmed community, including consumers overcharged at vertically integrated pharmacies [S2]

Covers every type of pharmacy — retail, mail-order, specialty, hospital, long-term care — and defines pharmacy benefit manager broadly so it captures middlemen regardless of what they call themselves [S2]

analysis.who_pays: The large vertically integrated health companies that own an insurer, a pharmacy benefit manager, and big pharmacy chains together. They would have to sell their pharmacy businesses within three years, and their pharmacy revenue during any violation period could be clawed back.
analysis.who_pays_short: Integrated insurers and pharmacy benefit managers

drawbacks.text: A forced breakup is disruptive: divesting hundreds or thousands of pharmacies over three years could create transitions that affect continuity of care for patients who use mail-order or specialty pharmacy services owned by their insurer [S2]

The integrated companies argue that combining insurance, benefit management, and pharmacies lowers costs through bargaining power and one-stop convenience, so a flat ownership ban removes a business model as well as an abuse of it (general knowledge about how vertical integration in drug supply is defended)

An ownership ban is an indirect tool for drug prices: it may change who captures the middleman margin without directly capping what patients pay, so relief for consumers would depend on new competition actually emerging

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real structural conflict: the company that negotiates drug prices, decides which pharmacies patients can use, and sells the drugs can rig the game in its own favor. The cost is that breaking up integrated companies takes years and the disruption falls partly on patients during the transition, and a three-year divestment clock is a blunt instrument compared with conduct-based rules. The core fix, though, goes at the root of the problem rather than the symptoms.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final weeks of the session and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which took no further action before that Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 11, 2024, by Rep. Diana Harshbarger with Rep. Jake Auchincloss, a Republican and a Democrat introducing it together [S2]
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S4]
No hearing, markup, or vote followed; the action history shows no action after the referral, and the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025 [S4]
The bill had two cosponsors, both Democrats [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large vertically integrated health companies keep their combined insurer-PBM-pharmacy businesses unchanged. Patients, community pharmacies, and antitrust enforcers got nothing from the 118th Congress.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 11, 2024 and never scheduled a hearing or markup before the Congress ended 23 days later

against.name: Vertically integrated insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
against.role: Companies that own an insurer, a PBM, and large pharmacy chains together (e.g., CVS Health, UnitedHealth, Cigna)
against.what_they_did: The bill would force divestment of their pharmacy businesses; such companies are prominent opponents of ownership-separation legislation, and the industry's opposition to PBM structural reforms is widely reported

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican and both cosponsors were Democrats, so the bill had a bipartisan sponsor team but so few members signed on that no partisan pattern had formed.

industries.industry: Vertically integrated insurers and PBMs (CVS Health, UnitedHealth/OptumRx, Cigna/Express Scripts)
industries.note: These companies own the health plan, the PBM that negotiates prices and steers patients, and major pharmacy and mail-order chains. The bill would force them to sell the pharmacies, ending a structure in which the referee of drug pricing also owns the players — a structure that lets them capture margins at both ends of a prescription. Their pharmacy revenue is the direct target of the ban and of the disgorgement provision.

Community pharmacies today compete for patients whose own insurer and PBM own rival pharmacies and decide whether they are in network. Ending common ownership removes the conflict that puts them at a structural disadvantage, and local pharmacies are often the lifeline for older and rural patients.
